cd /Users/bgauduch/git/oss/terraform-examples && gh issue create --title "feat(terraform-actions-lambda): illustrate the escape hatch with a case no native action covers" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Context

`examples/terraform-actions-lambda` demonstrates `action "aws_lambda_invoke"` as the generic escape hatch, and illustrates it with a DynamoDB on-demand backup. A native `aws_dynamodb_create_backup` action covers exactly that, so the illustration undercuts the point it makes: a reader can object that the escape hatch was never needed here.

The README currently states the trade-off (the backup reads in one screen and is checkable with one CLI call) and lists the cases that do justify the hatch. That is honest, not sufficient.

## Proposal

Swap the illustration for day-2 work with no provider action, the kind that used to live in `null_resource` + `local-exec` or in a pipeline step:

- seed reference data on creation, then backfill an attribute after a schema change,
- purge a CDN or WAF not hosted on AWS (Cloudflare, Fastly, Akamai),
- register a release or deployment marker in a third-party system,
- call an internal API to drain a component before it is replaced.

Preference goes to the data seeding + backfill: it stays self-contained (no third-party credentials, no account outside the sandbox), its effect is visible with a single `aws dynamodb scan`, and the wiring of the lab does not change, only the Lambda body.

## What makes it more than a Lambda swap

The two labs are deliberately paired on the event choice: `terraform-actions` runs `after_update` because an invalidation publishes a consequence of the change, this lab runs `before_update` because a backup protects against it. A backfill naturally belongs to `after_update`, so the pairing has to be reworked rather than inherited. Options to weigh when picking this up:

- keep `before_update` with a pre-migration export or a checkpoint written elsewhere,
- move to `after_update` and rebuild the companion narrative around a different contrast.

## Non-goals

- No credential or account outside the sandbox.
- The lab stays readable in one screen, with an effect checkable from the CLI.
EOF
)" 2>&1 | tail -2

content.text:
Les trois sont faits.

**Force-push** : 6 commits réécrits, contenu bit-à-bit identique (`git diff` vide contre l'ancienne tête), corps wrappés sous 100 caractères. `Conventional commits` passe en SUCCESS, PR #39 en `CLEAN`, prête à merger quand tu veux.

**Issue #40** ouverte : [illustrate the escape hatch with a case no native action covers](https://github.com/bgauduch/terraform-examples/issues/40). Elle trace le problème, les candidats, la préférence pour le seed + backfill, et surtout le piège : les deux labs sont appariés sur le choix d'événement, donc basculer sur un backfill (`after_update` par nature) demande de refondre le récit du couple, pas seulement le corps de la Lambda.

**Vault** : conducteur mis à jour et committé (preuve de cache en A1/A2, vocabulaire day-0/1/2 dans le WHY, réponse anticipée sur le choix de l'illustration en B1, état pre-flight réécrit).

## Un écart entre ce que tu m'as dit et ce que voit AWS

Tu as détruit **T1 uniquement**. Vérifié à l'instant :

| | État | `terraform plan` |
|---|---|---|
| T1 CloudFront + S3 | détruit, state local vide | `9 to add, 1 to invoke` |
| T2 DynamoDB + Lambda | **toujours déployé** | `No changes` |
| 8 backups DynamoDB | toujours là, 0 octet chacun | hors Terraform |

Rien de tout ça ne coûte (table à l'usage vide, Lambda au repos, backups à 0 octet), et garder T2 t'évite le redéploiement plus la contrainte DNS demain matin. Mais si ton intention était de tout raser, il reste T2 et les backups, ces derniers ne partant jamais avec un `destroy`.

**Demain matin** : `terraform apply` dans `examples/terraform-actions`, au moins 30 min avant 13h (2 min 42 pour la distribution plus la propagation), puis contrôle que le site sert v1. Le premier apply déclenche `after_create`, donc une première invalidation : c'est attendu, pas un raté. T2 n'a besoin de rien, sauf l'`export AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_CLOUDWATCH_LOGS` dans le terminal du live.

# Terraform pin for this example (tflint/trivy inherited from the repo-root mise.toml).
# The real apply tasks target the AWS account of $AWS_PROFILE.
# Tasks are ordered as the progressive demo stages (read the README "Progressive demo").
# Run with `mise run <task>`; list them with `mise tasks`. Tasks run in a subshell,
# so any `cd` inside a task never leaks into your interactive shell.
[tools]
terraform = "1.15.6"

[tasks.init]
description = "init (providers: aws + random)"
run = "terraform init"

[tasks.fmt]
description = "format check"
run = "terraform fmt -recursive -check -diff"

[tasks.validate]
description = "validate the config"
run = "terraform validate"

[tasks.test-validate]
description = "Stage 1 - variable validations only (expect_failures, creds-free)"
run = "terraform test -filter=tests/validations.tftest.hcl -verbose"

[tasks.test-plan]
description = "Stage 2 - mocked plan assertions only (mock_provider, creds-free)"
run = "terraform test -filter=tests/plan.tftest.hcl -verbose"

[tasks.test-fast]
description = "Stages 1+2 - creds-free layer (runs in CI without secrets)"
run = "terraform test -filter=tests/validations.tftest.hcl -filter=tests/plan.tftest.hcl -verbose"

[tasks.test-deploy]
description = "Stage 3 - integration: real apply on AWS (requires AWS_PROFILE set)"
run = "terraform test -filter=tests/deploy.tftest.hcl"

[tasks.test-parallel]
description = "Stage 4 - parallel + state_key: 2 concurrent deployments (requires AWS_PROFILE set)"
run = "terraform test -filter=tests/parallel.tftest.hcl"

[tasks.test]
description = "full suite (requires AWS_PROFILE set for the apply stages)"
run = "terraform test"

[tasks.sweep]
description = "clean up orphaned resources by tag (see sweep.sh)"
run = "./sweep.sh"

[tasks.clean]
description = "remove local terraform state"
run = "find . -type d -name '.terraform' -prune -exec rm -rf {} + ; find . -name '*.tfstate*' -delete"
=== sweep.sh ===
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Sweeper: cleans up orphaned test buckets (left by a `terraform test` interrupted
# before its auto-destroy). Targets resources carrying the suite tag.
# Tag source of truth: providers.tf (default_tags tftest-suite).
#
# Usage:
#   ./sweep.sh           # list tagged buckets (dry-run)
#   ./sweep.sh --force   # empty then delete each tagged bucket
#
# Requires AWS_PROFILE to be exported. Tooled alternative: aws-nuke / awsweeper
# filtered on the same tag.
set -euo pipefail

TAG_KEY="tftest-suite"
TAG_VALUE="terraform-module-testing"
REGION="${AWS_REGION:-eu-west-1}"
FORCE="${1:-}"

mapfile -t ARNS < <(aws resourcegroupstaggingapi get-resources \
  --region "$REGION" \
  --tag-filters "Key=${TAG_KEY},Values=${TAG_VALUE}" \
  --resource-type-filters "s3" \
  --query 'ResourceTagMappingList[].ResourceARN' --output text | tr '\t' '\n')

if [ "${#ARNS[@]}" -eq 0 ] || [ -z "${ARNS[0]:-}" ]; then
  echo "No bucket tagged ${TAG_KEY}=${TAG_VALUE}."
  exit 0
fi

echo "Tagged buckets found:"
printf '  %s\n' "${ARNS[@]}"

if [ "$FORCE" != "--force" ]; then
  echo "Dry-run. Re-run with --force to empty + delete."
  exit 0
fi

for arn in "${ARNS[@]}"; do
  bucket="${arn##*:::}"
  echo "Deleting ${bucket} ..."
  aws s3 rm "s3://${bucket}" --recursive >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
  aws s3api delete-bucket --bucket "${bucket}" --region "$REGION"
done
echo "Cleanup done."

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Sweeper: deletes the on-demand DynamoDB backups this lab's action created.
# `terraform destroy` removes the table but never its backups. On-demand backups
# outlive their table by design, and Terraform does not track them anyway since
# the Lambda creates them out of band. Destroy-time `action_trigger` events, which
# would let the lab clean up after itself, land in Terraform 1.16 (alpha).
#
# Usage:
#   ./sweep.sh           # list the backups (dry-run)
#   ./sweep.sh --force   # delete them
#
# Requires AWS_PROFILE to be exported. Runs before or after `terraform destroy`:
# the table name falls back to the `project` variable default once the state is gone.
# Override with TABLE_NAME=... or AWS_REGION=... if you changed the defaults.
set -euo pipefail

REGION="${AWS_REGION:-eu-west-1}"

# terraform-actions-lambda

> **Type**: `lab`
> **Tags**: `aws` `actions` `lambda` `dynamodb` `v1.14`

Terraform **1.14** actions can run **provider-native** side-effects (see `terraform-actions` for a
CloudFront invalidation). But the provider only ships a handful of native actions. This lab shows
the **escape hatch**: `action "aws_lambda_invoke"` lets a lifecycle event run **any logic you can
put in a Lambda**. The illustration: take a **timestamped on-demand DynamoDB backup** before
Terraform ever mutates the table.

> **Day 0 / day 1 / day 2**, since the whole point hangs on it: day 0 is design, day 1 is build and
> deploy, day 2 is everything after go-live (operate, evolve, repair). In Terraform terms, day 1
> creates the resource and day 2 is the work that keeps happening to it afterwards.

## The idea

```hcl
action "aws_lambda_invoke" "backup" {
  config {
    function_name   = aws_lambda_function.backup.function_name
    payload         = jsonencode({ table_name = local.table_name })
    invocation_type = "RequestResponse"
  }
}

resource "aws_dynamodb_table" "this" {
  # ...
  lifecycle {
    action_trigger {
      events  = [after_create, before_update]
      actions = [action.aws_lambda_invoke.backup]
    }
  }
}
```

The Lambda (`lambda/backup.py`) calls `dynamodb.create_backup(...)`, but it could run anything
else: a third-party API call, a Slack post, a data migration. That is the point.

## Why `before_update` and not `after_update`

The event you pick encodes the intent. `after_*` publishes a consequence of the change (the
companion `terraform-actions` lab invalidates a CDN cache *after* new content is uploaded).
`before_update` protects against the change: the snapshot is taken while the table is still in its
previous state, so an unwanted schema or capacity change is recoverable. In the apply output the
action completes **before** `Modifying...` on the table.

`after_create` still fires once, on creation: there is nothing to back up before a table exists.

> A native `aws_dynamodb_create_backup` action exists. Going through Lambda here demonstrates the
> generic mechanism. Reach for a native action first when one fits.

The backup is the illustration because it reads in one screen and its effect is checkable with one
CLI call. The escape hatch earns its keep on the day-2 work no provider action covers, the kind that
used to sit in a `null_resource` + `local-exec` or in a pipeline step bolted next to Terraform:

- purge a CDN or WAF you do not host (Cloudflare, Fastly, Akamai),
- seed reference data, or backfill an attribute after a schema change,
- register a release or a deployment marker in a third-party system,
- call an internal API to drain a component before it gets replaced.

Same wiring as below, only the Lambda body changes.

## Avoiding the dependency cycle

The table's `after_create` action invokes the Lambda, so the Lambda must **not** depend on the
table (that would be `table → action → lambda → table`). The Lambda's IAM policy therefore scopes
`dynamodb:CreateBackup` to an ARN built from `var.region` + the caller account id + the table name
(`local.table_arn`), not from `aws_dynamodb_table.this.arn`.

## What gets deployed

- A DynamoDB table (`PAY_PER_REQUEST`, point-in-time recovery + SSE enabled).
- A Python Lambda + least-privilege IAM role (`dynamodb:CreateBackup` on the table, write to its own
  log group) and an explicit CloudWatch log group with retention.

## Prerequisites

- **Terraform `>= 1.14.0`** (pinned to `1.14.9` via `mise.toml`; actions do not exist before 1.14).
- **AWS provider `6.41.0`** (carries the `aws_lambda_invoke` action).
- AWS credentials for `apply` (`validate`/`plan` need none). Default region: `eu-west-1`.

## Run (live demo)

```bash
terraform init
terraform apply        # creates the table + Lambda; after_create fires the FIRST backup.

# See the backup the action just created:
aws dynamodb list-backups --table-name "$(terraform output -raw table_name)" --region eu-west-1
```

Then, the day-2 change:

```bash
# Uncomment the `ttl` block on aws_dynamodb_table.this in main.tf, then:
terraform apply        # before_update fires a NEW timestamped backup, then the table is modified.
```

Pick a fast mutation to demo this: enabling TTL or changing tags settles in ~5 s, while adding a
global secondary index takes several minutes of `Still modifying...`.

TTL is rate-limited. `UpdateTimeToLive` takes up to an hour to fully process, and any further call on
the same table inside that window fails with a `ValidationException`
([API reference](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/APIReference/API_UpdateTimeToLive.html)).
Running the gesture twice in a row means waiting out the hour, or switching to a tag change.

Invoke the action **stand-alone** (back up on demand, no infra change):

```bash
terraform apply -invoke=action.aws_lambda_invoke.backup
```

Teardown:

```bash
terraform destroy      # on-demand backups survive table deletion; remove them manually if needed.
```

## Going further

- `terraform-actions`: the same mechanism with a native provider action (CloudFront), and the
  `after_update` counterpart of the event choice discussed above.

## Troubleshooting

- `dial tcp 0.0.0.0:443: connect: connection refused` on `logs.<region>.amazonaws.com`: a local
  DNS filter (Pi-hole, AdGuard, router-level ad blocking) is blackholing hostnames that start with
  `logs.`, so the log group resource fails on create and even on refresh. Point the SDK at the
  dual-stack endpoint, which resolves normally, in the shell that runs Terraform:

  ```bash
  export AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_CLOUDWATCH_LOGS=https://logs.eu-west-1.api.aws
  ```

  `AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_<SERVICE>` is the standard per-service override, where `<SERVICE>` is the API
  model `serviceId` uppercased with spaces turned into underscores
  ([SDK reference](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sdkref/latest/guide/feature-ss-endpoints.html)). It
  keeps the fix inside the repo instead of depending on the network you happen to sit behind.
  Allow-listing the endpoint on the resolver works too, when you own it.

content.text:
Le nettoyage est maintenant outillé, testé, et la raison de son existence est documentée.

**`examples/terraform-actions-lambda/sweep.sh`** (calqué sur `terraform-module-testing/sweep.sh`, le précédent du repo) : liste les backups par défaut, les supprime avec `--force`. Il fonctionne avant comme après le `destroy` puisque le nom de table retombe sur le défaut de la variable `project` quand le state a disparu. `TABLE_NAME` et `AWS_REGION` en override.

**Deux tâches mise** dans le lab :

```bash
mise run sweep       # dry-run, liste ce qui traîne
mise run teardown    # terraform destroy, puis sweep --force
```

**Le pourquoi, dans le README** : ce n'est pas un oubli du lab. Un backup on-demand survit à sa table par conception, et Terraform ne l'a jamais connu puisque la Lambda le crée hors de son champ. Aucun événement d'`action_trigger` actuel ne peut nettoyer non plus, les events destroy étant en 1.16 alpha. Autrement dit le trou est exactement celui que tu annonces en §Limites du live, et le sweeper est la réponse en attendant. C'est un point d'architecture à connaître avant de câbler une action qui crée quelque chose.

**Testé pour de vrai**, parce que le tien avait été vidé entre-temps et qu'un sweeper non exercé ne prouve rien :

```
invoke stand-alone   -> Action complete, 0 added, 0 changed, 0 destroyed
sweep.sh             -> 1 backup listé
sweep.sh --force     -> supprimé
sweep.sh             -> vide
terraform plan       -> No changes
```

L'état de départ de T2 est intact.

**PR #39** : titre passé en `feat(terraform-actions-lambda): sweep the backups destroy leaves behind`, puisque le squash-merge prend le titre et qu'un `docs` aurait masqué la tâche dans le changelog release-please. Corps réécrit pour couvrir le périmètre réel, avec un renvoi vers l'issue #40. CI verte, `CLEAN`, 7 commits.
